notes: Ruling slot 3: Tsiranana's PSD. No real coalition partner exists (PSD dominates the assembly); slot 18 holds MONIMA (Monja Jaona), the radical southern opposition. AKFM kept in MD slot 4 (pro-Soviet). MD slot 5 'Malagasy Revolutionary Party' (AREMA, 1976) is anachronistic and replaced by student radicals. Slot 7 is the Gendarmerie, slot 22 the armed forces under Gen. Ramanantsoa.

0.name: Mpiaro ny Repoblika
0.text:
Mpiaro ny Repoblika, 'the Guardians of the Republic', is the hardline wing of the ruling PSD gathered around André Resampa, the powerful Minister of the Interior and party secretary-general. Its prefects, police chiefs and party bosses run the provinces and treat every opposition meeting as a potential threat.

The faction wants firm one-party dominance, tight control of the press and the unions, and a resolutely anti-communist line backed by France and the United States. It distrusts the Merina opposition in Antananarivo and the radicals of the south alike, and its leverage lies in the interior ministry, the party apparatus and the provincial administration.

1.name: Eglizy Katolika eto Madagasikara
1.text:
The Catholic Church in Madagascar is the country's largest denomination, with strong roots among the coastal peoples and the Betsileo, a dense network of schools and a hierarchy now led by Jérôme Rakotomalala, Archbishop of Antananarivo, created the first Malagasy cardinal in 1969. Many PSD notables and civil servants were educated in its mission schools.

Its lay movements and press promote Christian democratic values: family, private schooling, social reform through cooperatives and resolute rejection of communism. The Church supports the Western orientation of the republic while criticising corruption and rural poverty, and its leverage lies in the schools, the parishes and its moral authority over millions of believers.

2.name: Ny Mpanavao
2.text:
Ny Mpanavao, 'the Reformers', are liberal-minded ministers, technocrats and businessmen inside and around the PSD who look to the poet and minister Jacques Rabemananjara, a veteran of the nationalist struggle of 1947, as their most eloquent figure. They want the regime to open up before it hardens into a party-state.

They favour a market economy, foreign investment, freedom of the press and an independent judiciary, alongside continued partnership with France and the West. Their base is the educated elite of the ministries, the chambers of commerce and the professions, and their leverage lies in competence the regime cannot do without.

3.name: Parti social-démocrate de Madagascar
3.text:
The Social Democratic Party was founded in 1956 by Philibert Tsiranana, a teacher from the north-west, as the party of the coastal peoples against Merina dominance. It has led Madagascar since independence in 1960, with Tsiranana as President of the Republic, and holds all but a handful of seats in the National Assembly.

The PSD preaches a moderate 'Malagasy socialism' of cooperatives and rural development while keeping close defence, monetary and economic ties with France and a firmly anti-communist, pro-Western foreign policy. Its strength lies in the provincial administration, the rural notables of the coast and its near monopoly of public office.

4.name: Antokon'ny Kongresin'ny Fahaleovantenan'i Madagasikara
4.english: Congress Party for the Independence of Madagascar
4.text:
The Congress Party for the Independence of Madagascar was founded in 1958 as a front of nationalists and Marxists and is led by Pastor Richard Andriamanjato, mayor of Antananarivo. It is the main legal opposition, holding the capital's city hall and a few seats in the National Assembly.

The AKFM demands an end to the French military bases and cooperation agreements, nationalisation of the great trading houses and land reform, and it aligns openly with the Soviet Union. Its base is the Merina intelligentsia, Protestant congregations and workers of the capital, and its leverage lies in Antananarivo, where the PSD has never been able to beat it.
4.wiki: Congress Party for the Independence of Madagascar

5.name: Tanora Revolisionera
5.text:
Tanora Revolisionera, 'the Revolutionary Youth', are student militants at the University of Madagascar and the lycées of Antananarivo, inspired by May 1968 in Paris, by Mao and by the anti-colonial wars of Africa and Asia. They despise the PSD as a French puppet and the AKFM as too timid.

They demand the Malagasisation of education, an end to the cooperation agreements and French bases, and a socialist revolution carried by students, workers and the unemployed youth of the capital. Their leverage lies in their ability to fill the streets of Antananarivo and to shut down the schools on which the regime's elite depends.

6.name: Mpiaro ny Tanindrazana
6.text:
Mpiaro ny Tanindrazana, 'the Defenders of the Ancestral Land', gathers veterans of the 1947 insurrection, traditional healers and village elders who see independence as unfinished while French soldiers, settlers and companies remain. They honour the dead of the uprising and the ancestors above any imported ideology.

They want the French expelled, foreign land returned, ancestral custom restored over Western law and Madagascar aligned with the anti-imperialist states, without any taste for Marxist atheism. Their leverage lies in the rural east and in the moral authority of the 1947 fighters, whose memory no Malagasy politician can afford to insult.

7.name: Zandarimariam-pirenena
7.text:
The National Gendarmerie is the rural police force of the republic, stationed in every district and better spread across the island than the army. Its rising Malagasy officers, among them Richard Ratsimandrava, resent the French advisers and the corruption of PSD officials they are asked to protect.

A current among these officers dreams of a disciplined, austere state rebuilt on the fokonolona village communities, free of French tutelage and open to the non-aligned and socialist world. Its leverage lies in armed posts throughout the countryside and in a reputation for honesty that the politicians of the capital lack.

8.name: Khoja Shia Ithna'ashari Jamaat
8.text:
The Khoja Shia Ithna'ashari Jamaat organises the Twelver Shia families of Indian origin who settled in Madagascar from Gujarat and became prominent merchants in Mahajanga, Antananarivo and the western ports. Its community councils run mosques, schools and welfare funds and keep links with the federation of Khoja jamaats in East Africa.

The jamaat favours an educated, reform-minded faith, modern schooling and loyal cooperation with the authorities. Its members, often denied citizenship and exposed to resentment as 'Karana', seek security for their businesses and residence rights, and their leverage lies in their weight in import-export trade and credit.

9.name: Ansar-e-Wilayat
9.text:
Ansar-e-Wilayat is a small circle of young Shia men in Mahajanga who studied in Najaf and Karachi and returned convinced that their merchant elders have bartered faith for commerce. They meet apart from the community councils, around the sermons of militant clergy from Iraq and Iran.

They hold that the learned clergy must guide Muslim life, denounce the Shah and his Western patrons, and call for strict observance and separation from non-Muslim society. Without status in the community or in Malagasy politics, their leverage is limited to a few families and to correspondence with radical clerical networks abroad.

10.name: Antalaotra
10.text:
The Antalaotra are the old Swahili-Malagasy Muslim communities of the north-west coast, joined by the large Comorian population of Mahajanga and Antsiranana. Their notables and Shafi'i teachers run the mosques and Koranic schools of the port towns and have dealt with every ruler of the island for centuries.

They are quietist and loyal to the government, asking for freedom of worship, Koranic schooling and protection for Comorian traders and dockworkers, whose presence breeds friction with local Malagasy. Their leverage lies in their numbers in the western ports and in links to the Comoros, Zanzibar and the Arab world.

11.name: Jamaat-e-Khilafat
11.text:
Jamaat-e-Khilafat is a tiny clandestine group of young Comorian and Indian-origin Muslims in Mahajanga who have encountered Hizb ut-Tahrir pamphlets and pan-Islamic radio broadcasts through contacts in East Africa and the Gulf. It meets in back rooms of the port quarter.

Its members reject nation-states, elections and both superpowers, and preach the restoration of a single caliphate for all Muslims. In Madagascar they can do little beyond study circles and recruitment among dockworkers and students, but they believe that the Muslim ports of the Indian Ocean will one day rise with the rest of the umma.

12.name: Shabab al-Islah
12.text:
Shabab al-Islah, 'the Reform Youth', is an association of educated young Comorian and Malagasy Muslims in Mahajanga and Antananarivo, many of them students returned from Cairo, who read Hasan al-Banna and want an organised, socially active Islam. They are impatient with both the traditional notables and the merchant elite.

The association promotes Islamic schools, welfare, Arabic teaching and moral reform, accepts constitutional politics and supports the Palestinian and Arab causes. Neutral between the blocs, it seeks a recognised voice for Muslims in Malagasy public life, and its leverage lies in its schools and its growing following among Comorian youth.

13.name: Ny Fitondrana
13.text:
Ny Fitondrana, 'the Administration', is the corps of prefects, sub-prefects, district chiefs and senior civil servants who actually run the Malagasy Republic, largely trained by the French and still advised by French officials. Under the PSD they have become the true government of the countryside.

They care less for ideology than for order: tax collection, forced cultivation targets, roads and statistics, with no taste for either Moscow or open democracy. Their leverage lies in the power to levy taxes, assign land, call up labour and decide which villages receive schools, clinics and roads.

14.name: Fiangonan'i Jesoa Kristy eto Madagasikara
14.english: Church of Jesus Christ in Madagascar
14.text:
The Church of Jesus Christ in Madagascar was formed in 1968 by the union of the island's main Reformed and Congregational churches, heirs of the London Missionary Society that converted the Merina monarchy in the nineteenth century. It is the spiritual home of the Merina elite and many highland villages.

The church stands for Protestant morality, education and national dignity, and keeps its distance from the Catholic-leaning PSD while avoiding open partisanship. Several of its pastors sympathise with the AKFM, yet its congregations are largely conservative, and its leverage lies in its schools, its press and the loyalty of the highlands.
14.wiki: Church of Jesus Christ in Madagascar

15.name: Les Grandes Compagnies
15.text:
Les Grandes Compagnies are the old French trading houses, above all the Compagnie Marseillaise de Madagascar and the Compagnie Lyonnaise, which still dominate the export of vanilla, coffee, cloves and sugar and the import of manufactured goods ten years after independence. French banks and plantation companies stand beside them.

They want the cooperation agreements, the franc zone and the open economy preserved, and they quietly finance politicians who defend them against nationalisation. Their leverage lies in controlling credit, shipping and the island's foreign trade, which no Malagasy government can replace overnight.

16.name: Ny Karana
16.text:
Ny Karana are the Indian-origin merchant families, Muslim and Hindu, who run much of the retail, textile and collection trade of the western and northern towns, alongside Chinese shopkeepers on the east coast. Many hold French or British papers rather than Malagasy citizenship.

They want free trade, low taxes, easy credit and protection of property, and fear both nationalisation and popular resentment against foreign traders. Avoiding open politics, they lend money to officials and politicians of every camp, and their leverage lies in the rural collection of vanilla, rice and cattle that passes through their shops.

17.name: Mpiaro ny Ala
17.text:
Mpiaro ny Ala, 'the Forest Protectors', is a network of Malagasy foresters, naturalists of the Tsimbazaza botanical and zoological park and foreign scientists alarmed by the destruction of the island's unique forests through tavy slash-and-burn farming, logging and charcoal burning. They warn that lemurs and countless species exist nowhere else on earth.

They call for new reserves, protection of the eastern rainforest and the western dry forests, reforestation and research partnerships with international bodies. Their leverage lies in scientific prestige and foreign interest, though they struggle against peasants' need for land and the government's hunger for timber revenue.

18.name: Madagasikara Otronin'ny Malagasy
18.english: National Movement for the Independence of Madagascar
18.text:
MONIMA, the National Movement for the Independence of Madagascar, was founded in 1958 by Monja Jaona, a veteran nationalist from the deep south. It is the voice of the impoverished peasants and herders of Toliara province and the fiercest opposition to Tsiranana's government outside the capital.

The movement denounces the tax burden, forced labour practices, drought relief failures and the abuses of PSD officials in the south, and calls for a radical, non-aligned socialism and an end to French control of the economy. Its leverage lies in the southern countryside, where poverty and anger at the administration are deep.

19.name: Tolom-bahoaka
19.text:
Tolom-bahoaka, 'the People's Struggle', are Maoist circles of teachers, students and young AKFM dissidents in Antananarivo and Toliara who regard the pro-Soviet Congress party as bourgeois and too comfortable in the capital's city hall. They study the Little Red Book and the peasant revolution of China.

They call for a people's war led from the countryside, total rupture with France, land to the tillers and alliance with China and the Third World against both superpowers. Their leverage lies in student committees and in contacts with the southern peasant movement, where their ideas find a readier audience.

20.name: Le Front Côtier
20.text:
Le Front Côtier, 'the Coastal Front', is a populist current among the côtier peoples who fear a return of Merina domination and see the highland elite of Antananarivo as heirs of the old kingdom that once conquered them. It finds voices among PSD backbenchers and provincial notables.

It demands that jobs, scholarships and promotions be reserved for côtiers, that Merina influence in the administration and the opposition be curbed, and that foreign traders be restricted. Fervently anti-communist, it treats the AKFM as a Merina plot, and its leverage lies in mobilising ethnic fears in every coastal province.

21.name: Les Ultras
21.text:
Les Ultras are the hardline French settlers, planters and ex-soldiers of the colonial era, some of them veterans of Indochina and Algeria, who never accepted Malagasy independence. Concentrated on the plantations of the east coast and the north, they meet in veterans' associations and clubs.

They want French troops and settlers to stay for good, nationalist agitators crushed by force and the republic kept as a dependency of France, and they despise both Malagasy nationalism and democracy. Their leverage lies in their estates, weapons and friends in the French military establishment still stationed on the island.

22.name: Tafika Malagasy
22.text:
The Malagasy Armed Forces were formed at independence in 1960 from Malagasy units of the French army and are commanded by General Gabriel Ramanantsoa, chief of the general staff. They remain small and dependent on French training, equipment and the large French base at Diego-Suarez.

The officer corps sees itself as a neutral guardian of the nation above party and ethnic quarrels, discreetly critical of PSD corruption and of the regime's dependence on France. Its leverage lies in its discipline, its prestige among the Merina elite from which many officers come, and the possibility of acting as arbiter in a crisis.

23.name: Ny Andriana
23.text:
Ny Andriana are the descendants of the Merina nobility and the royal lineages of the kingdom of Madagascar, abolished by France in 1897 when Queen Ranavalona III was sent into exile. Their families remain prominent in the highlands, the Protestant church and the professions.

A nostalgic circle among them cherishes the Rova palace and the memory of the old kingdom and dreams of national unity under a restored crown or at least of honour for the royal heritage. With the côtier peoples hostile to any Merina revival, their leverage lies in lineage, wealth and the prestige of Antananarivo's ancient families.
